To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
discrete breathers can be found in proteins, they are stable and can be excited, and they can be used to control protein dynamics.

(i) localized vibrational modes of a realistic protein model are time-periodic nonlinear solutions of the underlying equations of motion; (ii) these modes are resilient to external perturbations and mediate efficient energy transfer in the protein, thus providing a mechanism for remote energy accumulation and conformational changes; and (iii) the nonlinear dynamics is accompanied by a static distortion of the protein structure, which can be used to control local conformational transitions in proteins.
discrete breathers emerge in a coarse-grained model protein and that these nonlinear localized modes are able to concentrate energy for a long time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of discrete nonlinear modes in proteins.
the study of the dynamics of a protein model featuring realistic physical interactions and a realistic amino-acid sequence, in the presence of a perturbation.
the emergence and properties of DBs in a coarse-grained protein model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of DBs in a coarse-grained model is a consequence of the physical force-field and the amino acid sequence of the protein.
DBs are a natural consequence of the nonlinear dynamics of realistic coarse-grained proteins.
the presence of DBs in proteins is an important feature that may play a role in protein dynamics and function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DBs can be used as an energy storage and transfer device, which may provide an alternative mechanism to the traditional allosteric regulation of proteins.
the nonlinear dynamics of proteins is more than a mathematical curiosity: it is a key factor in the way proteins function and evolve.
the DBs are a natural and efficient means for the transfer of energy in proteins and that their presence is likely to have important biological implications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DBs can be viewed as a new type of dynamical defect in proteins, which may have a bearing on the mechanisms of protein folding, unfolding, and conformational transitions.
DBs may provide a new mechanism for energy storage in proteins.
the presence of DBs in proteins is a natural consequence of their nonlinear, discrete nature, rather than an exotic feature that needs to be specially engineered into them.
